subject: Architecture
title: The British Museum: The World Under One Roof
description: A quick, practical guide to The British Museum: The World Under One Roof.

hook.text: The British Museum has 8 million objects. Only 1% are on display at any time.

buildup.text: Founded in 1753, it was the world's first public national museum — free from day one.

discovery.text: Norman Foster's glass roof over the Great Court created Europe's largest covered public square.

twist.text: Many countries demand their artifacts back. The Rosetta Stone and Parthenon Marbles are bitterly disputed.

climax.text: It remains free to enter and attracts 6 million visitors per year — more than any UK attraction.

punchline.text: Free to enter. Priceless to debate.

quiz.question: What is special about the British Museum's admission policy since 1753?
options: Only British citizens are admitted free
It has always been free to enter
Admission is free only on Sundays

details.summary: The British Museum's Great Court, designed by Norman Foster and opened in 2000, transformed a neglected courtyard into Europe's largest covered public square with a tessellated glass roof of 3,312 unique triangular panels.
details.whyItMatters: The Great Court proves that architectural interventions can revitalize historic buildings. By covering an unused space with a structurally innovative roof.
takeaways: 3,312 unique triangular glass panels form Europe's largest covered square
No two panels are the same shape — each was computer-designed
The intervention doubled accessible museum space without altering the original

faq.question: How was the glass roof's geometry designed?
faq.answer: The roof spans between the circular Reading Room and the rectangular courtyard walls. Computer algorithms generated the optimal mesh of triangles to smoothly transition between these two geometries while minimizing steel weight and maximizing glass transparency. Each of the 3,312 panels is unique.

faq.question: What was in the Great Court before the roof?
faq.answer: The courtyard surrounding the Reading Room had been filled with book stacks for the British Library. When the library moved to its own building in 1997, the space was empty. Foster's roof transformed this forgotten gap into the museum's dramatic central gathering space.
